fixes.explanation: Yes, friend. "When the righteous flourish, the people rejoice, but when the wicked rule, the people groan." The proverb sets two situations side by side, and each one has its own sound. Same people, two very different sounds, and what changes is who's in charge.

Yes, friend. "A servant pampered from his youth will bring grief in the end." Notice the words in the end. It starts in his youth and lands at the end, kind of like a batch that only tells you how it went when it comes out of the oven. The proverb gives you the whole timeline in one breath.

Yes, friend. "Many seek the ruler’s favor, but a man receives justice from the LORD." The verse says many seek the ruler's favor, and then it turns. Seeking a ruler's favor and receiving justice are two different things here. The verse points your eyes past the ruler to the LORD.

I get the second-guessing, friend, but the proverb says exactly that: "An evil man is caught by his own sin…" The verse then flips to the righteous one, who sings and rejoices. I sat stuck in the back of a junk drawer for years, and let me tell you, being stuck is not a singing situation. Good thing the singing goes to the righteous one.

That's the one, friend. "…but blessed is he who keeps the Law." Where there is no vision, the people cast off restraint, and I picture a kitchen with no timer and everybody doing whatever they want. Then comes that little word but, and the blessing lands on the one who keeps the Law.

Yes, it's true, friend. "…a humble spirit will obtain honor." Pride is the one that brings a man low, and humble is the one that gets the honor. I've been low myself, all the way back in a junk drawer, so trust me, honor is the better deal.
